entries.title: Jodi Picoult: ‘Reading Ta-Nehisi Coates made me rethink racism’

entries.content:
My favourite book growing up

I loved Maurice Sendak’s Where the Wild Things Are. Max’s visit to the land of monsters is escapist, of course, but there’s darkness and poetry in it, too. “The walls became the world all around” has always stuck with me.

The book that changed me as a teenager

A Tree Grows in Brooklyn by Betty Smith. My mom gave it to me at around 12 or 13, and I remember thinking it was such an adult book at the time. It gave me a protagonist to admire who thrived in spite of the setbacks in her life, and also helped put into perspective the charmed life I’d been living.

The writer who changed my mind

Ta-Nehisi Coates. When I read Between the World and Me in 2015, I was working on a book about white privilege (and its flip side, racism), Small Great Things. I had truly believed myself to not be a racist in my everyday life, and reading Coates inspired me to attend social justice workshops. I came to understand there is a difference between being “not a racist” and being antiracist. One is passive, the other is active.

The book that made me want to be a writer

Gone With the Wind by Margaret Mitchell. I read it at 13 and memorised huge swaths of the book (which also explains why I didn’t have a boyfriend until I was 15). I distinctly remember looking up from the text when she described Atlanta burning, because the image she had crafted of the war and the smoke and the injured soldiers was so real I could smell and see and taste it. I thought: “She created a world out of words. I could do that, too.”

The author I came back to

Dostoevsky. I tried in high school, and then again in college. It’s just a lot of very long names and philosophical rants that seemingly go nowhere, punctuated by the occasional murder or suicide. I admit that when my eldest son took a high school course on Russian lit, I tried for a third time and … nope.

The book I reread

When I was in high school, I read Almost Paradise by Susan Isaacs every other year or so. It’s the only book I’ve repeated multiple times. It’s a comfort read about a midwestern part-Jewish girl who marries the Wasp of her dreams, and the life that follows afterward. I think at that time I was trying to imagine a love that encompassing, one that transcended backgrounds. I was going to Princeton, I was surrounded by trust fund babies, children of politicians, people who used “summer” as a verb. I was very much the outsider, and like Jane in this book, I wanted to believe that didn’t matter in the long run. (I wound up happily marrying a Wasp from Princeton. So maybe this book was not just a comfort read, but a how-to primer.)

The book I could never read again

I have to choose Gone With the Wind again, with a special side mention to Ta-Nehisi Coates and all the others who made me realise that the stereotypical portrait of Black people in this book is something I should have noticed the first time around.

The book I discovered later in life

The Book Thief by Markus Zusak. Using Death as a narrator is such a bold move, and making Death compassionate rather than terrifying is an even bolder one. Ironically, I now know this book as well as I know any of my own. For the past eight years I’ve been adapting it as a musical, which has been even more rewarding.

The book I am currently reading

I’ve just finished Everything Was Beautiful and Nothing Hurt by Ben Reeves. It, too, personifies death, but in a very different way. It’s a beautiful exploration of loss, grief and what it means to be human.

My comfort read

Anything by Alice Hoffman. Her novels are full of magical realism, and she makes writing look easy when it’s never easy. Her books feel like home to me.

entries.title: Green Kingdom by Ben Dark review – a luscious natural history of plant life
entries.summary: A gardener traces the dynasties that dominate the vegetal world in appropriately sumptuous proseJohn Ruskin, the Victorian writer and critic, hated the way science insisted on turning his beloved natural world into something smutty. entries.content:
John Ruskin, the Victorian writer and critic, hated the way science insisted on turning his beloved natural world into something smutty. Botanists, he complained, used “microscopic malice” to reduce the spurs, petals and stamens of his favourite flowers to “obscene processes and prurient apparitions”. Others were less squeamish. In 1908, Marie Stopes, the scientist who later became a champion of birth control, spent three days in Japan’s Matsushima Bay in a state of “grand excitement” hunting ginkgo sperms. Oliver Sacks, the neurologist, passed his adolescence at Kew gawping at the cycads’ sexual organs. Reading Ben Dark’s excellent account, it is hard not to conclude that even the most modest plants are living in a state of permanent arousal.

Each of Dark’s chapters tells the story of one plant dynasty, from rootless, seedless pond scum to alpine meadows. Some 97% of all the species that have ever existed are already extinct, but traces of them live on in their descendants, and it is these ancient threads that Dark pursues in this absorbing book. He is a professional gardener, yet his tastes run to the surprisingly sludgy. Orchids and roses have their place in the Green Kingdom, but nothing thrills him more than an evil-looking pond, rich in microscopic nutrients.

Sometimes Dark follows plants out of the botany books and into folklore. Overlay a map of Britain’s dragon legends with its coal seams, he explains, and the two match perfectly, from the Scottish Borders to south Wales. Take the Lambton Worm, the eel-like creature hooked in a County Durham brook by young John Lambton, a medieval boy who flung the creature down a well in disgust. There it grew monstrous enough to coil “in glistening black seams” around a hill, until Lambton, now a knight home from crusade, hacked it to pieces in the River Wear. In 1820 the antiquarian Robert Surtees remembered being shown a lump of the worm’s skin “rough and patterned like bull hide”. It was almost certainly a fossilised lycophyte, one of the giant clubmoss trees whose remains became the region’s coal.

Elsewhere, history needs no such embellishment. In Hiroshima, Dark visits Shukkeien, a centuries-old garden laid waste in August 1945 by the atomic bomb. The only survivors were a single pine and a ginkgo. Stripped bare by the blast, the ginkgo had nonetheless leafed out again by the end of that terrible summer. This means that buried in its trunk will be a double ring, “the record of a year in which life stopped and restarted”. No matter how many centuries the tree endures, it will always carry the record of that skipped heartbeat.

Some of this material has been covered many times before, but what lifts the book is Dark’s writing, which would have gladdened Ruskin’s crabby heart. Mosses sit on the earth “as toupées for the world’s scalp”; Colocasia esculenta has “leaves like Norman shields”; “civilisations disappear, ice shrinks away and the campanula abides”. Dark has a sharp eye for the startling detail too: giant bamboo can grow a metre a day and the stalks weigh the same as an Asian elephant.

Beneath the pleasures of Green Kingdom runs a serious argument about how we come to know the natural world. The book opens with the wartime destruction of the Berlin-Dahlem Botanical Museum’s collections, in which 3.5 million specimens were burned in a single night. These were the life’s work of the “miners of science”, the patient classifiers who catalogued the plant world one dried sprig at a time. By the time of its destruction, such painstaking work had come to seem “flabby and washed-out”. Since then DNA sequencing has begun to cast “a bright torch” through the tree of life. All the same, argues Dark, it cannot convey the beauty of an orchid’s “white petals above a burnt-caramel lip”.

This is a tad ironic. Having spent much of the book rebutting Ruskin’s nostalgia, Dark ends by remaking the Victorian critic’s case against a new and powerful way of understanding the natural world. His plea for a practice of close-looking and enduring wonder is hard to dismiss. For, as he puts it with characteristic pithiness, “plants are easy to love, data is sterile”.

entries.title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup
entries.summary: The Taper Man by Nick Harkaway; Watch the Quiet Snow by Mick Herron; Revenge Plot by Stephanie Wrobel; The Voices of the Dead by Nicola Upson; The Bells of Fortune by Leonora NattrassThe Taper Man by Nick Harkaway (Viking, £22) The second George Smiley continuation novel from John le Carré’s son Nick Harkaway is set in 1965 and features early iterations of several characters who appear in Tinker T
entries.content:
The Taper Man by Nick Harkaway (Viking, £22)

The second George Smiley continuation novel from John le Carré’s son Nick Harkaway is set in 1965 and features early iterations of several characters who appear in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and Smiley’s People. The cold war is at its height, and British intelligence is keen to protect one of its most important sources, Red Army general Vladimir Vasilev. When a colleague is shot in Helsinki, Smiley discovers a connection to a group of Soviet agents who, through their links to a now defunct spying operation in the US, may jeopardise this key asset. Smiley travels to California to find the “Taper Man”, a sleeper agent whose job is to remain behind when the rest of the network is burned. Meanwhile, leftwing academic Roy Bland goes undercover in Moscow, but things do not go according to plan. Intricately plotted and densely written, The Taper Man takes time to get going, with a fair bit of cold war history and analysis to be digested, but it is a worthy and welcome addition to the le Carré canon.

Watch the Quiet Snow by Mick Herron (Baskerville, £22)

This beautifully presented collection of previously published novellas is the perfect Christmas present for fans of Slow Horses. Two of the stories shed further light on Slough House supremo Jackson Lamb – “a grubby Santa, putting the grot into grotto” – and his shared past with MI5 archivist Molly Doran, while the other three take us into the farther reaches of Herron’s espionage world, where washed-up boozehound John Bachelor works as a “milkman”, looking after retired assets who have “come in from other nations’ colds”. Bachelor’s needs may be simple – shelter, and enough money to pickle himself in peace – but his drunken stumbles into the murky world of double and even triple agents invariably lead to complications and the unwelcome attention of fearsome Service chief Diana Taverner. With Herron’s trademark blend of cynical humour, sinister undercurrents, suspense, irony and pathos, this is a splendid read for a dark night.

Revenge Plot by Stephanie Wrobel (Michael Joseph, £18.99)

It’s Christmas, and literary agent Claudia Conley has rented a remote Catskills treehouse for solo festivities. Not only does she have family problems, she also has money worries, the sales of books by her star author Jo Stone, whose true identity is a closely guarded secret, having declined dramatically. Heavy snowfall means that when aspiring writer Arnie Tenderton deliberately crashes his car on Christmas morning, Claudia, unaware of the subterfuge, feels obliged to invite him and his young passenger to share her dinner. It gradually becomes clear that Arnie, who is determined to get Claudia to read his manuscript, isn’t just a fanatical wannabe author. He knows Jo Stone’s secret, and, as the revelations start to pile up, Claudia realises that she’s about to lose everything she’s worked so hard to build. Tense and pacey, this is a well-executed, bittersweet tale of ambition, artistic integrity, trauma appropriation and collusion, with plenty of entertaining side-eye directed at the publishing industry.

The Voices of the Dead by Nicola Upson (Faber, £16.99)

The latest instalment in Upson’s impressive Josephine Tey series takes the real-life mystery writer, here turned detective, from the horrors of the May 1941 London blitz to Portmeirion in north Wales. Detective chief inspector Archie Penrose is there on honeymoon, and Noël Coward is finishing his latest comedy, Blithe Spirit, but the relative peace doesn’t last: the National Gallery’s precious paintings are being hidden in a nearby slate mine, a woman’s skeleton is discovered, and Tey and Penrose find themselves investigating a 40-year-old mystery in the midst of a tight-knit community. Psychics have become popular during the trauma of wartime, and the eponymous voices help to cast light on proceedings. In plot terms, it’s a slow start, with the body not discovered until a third of the way through, but Upson’s skill at evoking the febrile, make-do atmosphere of wartime Britain is consummate, and the pages fly by.

The Bells of Fortune by Leonora Nattrass (Viper, £18.99)

This is the second 18th-century outing for Susan Bell, daughter of the former dean of Westminster. Effectively exiled to his brother’s Leicestershire seat after a minor royal scandal in 1774, Reverend Bell has obtained employment as tutor to Francis, the wayward son of prime minister Lord North. Susan is less than impressed by the tedium of rural life, which is enlivened only by her voluble parrot, Cuthbert, and her uncle’s dispute over waterways with his neighbour, the Earl of Stamford, who is intent on creating a canal system. When a visiting surveyor disappears, he’s presumed to have drowned, and an antiquarian’s claims that he must be lost in a network of tunnels that form the tomb of a mythical king are met with scepticism. But then young Francis also vanishes … Suitably gothic in ingredients and atmosphere, this is a well-researched historical mystery with an appealing narrator in the wry, sharply observant Susan.

entries.title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison
entries.summary: This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attentionAmerican author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery
entries.content:
American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing.

The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suzanna’s visits take increasingly constrained forms. Abjuring ordinary teenage activities, she takes the train towards the hill every Saturday, submits to searches, and follows rules about how to move and what and whom she may not touch.

Time passes most visibly in Suzanna’s grandmother’s body, the passage towards death harder to deny than the passage towards adulthood. The grandmother, herself a sometime communist with vivid memories of a trip to Russia as a young mother, lives surrounded by friends who are similarly jaded – war-weary Jewish radical thinkers in old age, looking back together on children mostly estranged, dead or far away; husbands who in various ways did not stay the course; wars and regimes more or less survived. Whatever care they receive comes from each other and rarely with good grace. The liveliest conversations – often darkly funny – are about what, if anything, daughters owe to not-good-enough mothers.

Perhaps surprisingly, this isn’t a question that preoccupies Suzanna, who has difficulty acknowledging her own agency. Practically competent as her situation requires her to be, she does not want to ascend the ladder of secondary education or break free from a mother who has no freedom. In some ways, the novel’s tight spatial and temporal circles reminded me of Solvej Balle’s On the Calculation of Volume, in which the same day replays itself for the same people in the same place. Suzanna, whose origin story is abandonment, whose estrangement from her mother runs wide and deep, is in many ways arrested, willing immobility in a small world whose narrowness is no protection from time.

This is, broadly, realist fiction. The material of low-budget, low-energy domesticity is vivid: smelly bedding, mucky floors, stale food. Avoiding sensationalism, Clark writes more about the low-key, cumulative humiliations and discomforts of incarceration than the horror, which is more effective for its shadowiness. A woman newly released from months of strip-lit solitary confinement keeps asking “what time is this”: the worst punishment seems to be the physical manifestation of the timelessness Suzanna craves.

Almost all the physical journeys in The Hill are between the apartment and the prison, mostly by train. The train is another enclosed, shared space, the time on it both liminal and definitive. This feels like a closed-room novel, but it isn’t, or not much more than most novels are. We move from one confinement to another, and back.

It took me a few chapters to trust that the novel was teaching me how to read it. There is much conversation, or at least many interweaving monologues from hard-bitten old women, many of whom speak elliptically, leaving Suzanna and the reader to work out the relevance or significance of half-anecdotes from decades gone by. No one goes anywhere or does anything new, and a lot of the talk is rambling. But it coalesces round incidents and themes, and moments of sharp comedy emerge, as when the grandmother remembers her own mother. “There was nothing like this ridiculously elegant woman weeping into a handkerchief to make life in Stalin’s starving land seem both manageable and promising.” (Not spoiler: wrong.)

The wildness, the light in the cracks, comes from animals that verge on the magical: semi-feral cats enacting a child’s repressed rage, guide dogs in training being fiercely loved in prison and, finally, magnificently, a parrot that can’t fly pacing the aisle of an aeroplane beside a mother in shackles. Read this novel playfully, slowly, with an open mind. It rewards attention.

entries.title: Hannah Lillith Assadi wins US National book award for ‘visionary’ novel Paradiso 17
entries.summary: Assadi’s third novel was inspired by the story of her late father, a Palestinian who escaped the Nakba as a child in 1948Palestinian-Jewish author Hannah Lillith Assadi has won the National book award for fiction, one of the US’s most prestigious literary prizes, for her novel Paradiso 17.Assadi’s third novel is a study of the psychic toll of displacement on migrants, through the tale of a Palesti
entries.content:
Palestinian-Jewish author Hannah Lillith Assadi has won the National book award for fiction, one of the US’s most prestigious literary prizes, for her novel Paradiso 17.

Assadi’s third novel is a study of the psychic toll of displacement on migrants, through the tale of a Palestinian man who escaped the Nakba in 1948, when more than 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes by Israel. The story was inspired by her father, Sami Abdul-Fattah Al-Assadi, who fled the Nakba as a child with his family, before studying in Italy and moving to New York.

In a tearful speech, Assadi said, “What a beautiful story this has been, from its origins at my father’s deathbed until now, ending here and accepting this award. And so full of pain.

“In the course of its writing, I have experienced deep personal grief and unimaginable collective grief. I have watched cancer ravage my father’s body and genocide ravage his people and their children. And perhaps this is the Palestinian story on this earth. So beautiful. So painful.”

The judges praised Assadi’s “elegant lyricism” and “ambitious bending of time and space” and called the novel “a visionary, finely wrought portrait of rupture and endurance”.

Assadi won the $10,000 prize against Edwidge Danticat’s Dèy, Julián Delgado Lopera’s Pretend You’re Dead and I Carry You, Valeria Luiselli’s Beginning Middle End and Morgan Thomas’ Mad Eden.

Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy won the $10,000 nonfiction prize for his debut Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, about his six years as a political prisoner in Egypt. ElGendy was unable to attend the ceremony after being denied a visa to the US, so his prize was collected by his editor Helen Thomaides, who read out his speech.

ElGendy said he had dreamed of turning his experience into a memoir as it gave him distance from the physical abuse he endured, and revealed he had practised award acceptance speeches under his duvet in prison.

“Today that dream should have come full circle but, like so many of the circles ruptured in my life, it will remain unfinished, broken by an oppressive regime with a fascist ideology whose concentration camps stand ready to swallow the bodies it deems undesirable,” ElGendy wrote.

The New York Times speculated earlier this month that ElGendy was not even eligible for the award as he did not meet its citizenship or residency requirements after fleeing the US due to Ice deportations, but the National Book Foundation, which administers the National book Awards, disputed this and said it did not “have any concerns regarding the eligibility of his title”.

Samar Yazbek of Syria, a finalist for the books in translation category, was also denied a visa, with the National Book Foundation describing both decisions as “unjust”.

The state department declined to comment on any specific cases, but issued a statement to Associated Press saying that “the Trump Administration continues to put America and its interests first by fully enforcing US immigration laws and ensuring lawful travel through our visa process. As Secretary [of State Marco] Rubio said, ‘a visa is a privilege, not a right’.”

Publishers submitted 1,912 books to the National book awards this year, with the winners judged by panels of authors, editors, booksellers and others in the literary community.

Brenda Hillman won the $10,000 poetry category for Still House in the Desert: An eco-contemplation, praised as “a rigorously unsentimental portrait of the stillness … of the poet’s childhood home after her mother’s death”.

David Leviathan and Gabriel Duckels won the $10,000 young people’s literature category for The Fight of Our Lives: AIDS in America.

Indian-British author Salman Rushdie was presented with a medal for “distinguished contribution to American letters”, while paediatrician and author Perri Klass was honoured for “outstanding service to the American literary community”.

Rushdie recalled being welcomed into the US literary scene after spending years under police protection in London after the fatwa over The Satanic Verses, and used his speech to thank the late Ursula K Le Guin for liking his first novel. “She was just about the only one who did! And it meant everything to me,” he said, to laughs.

“All I want to say is that it has been quite a ride, from over there to over here,” he added. “And to ride into this town and end up in this saloon, with these companions, is a hell of a thing.”

Actor and author Kyle MacLachlan hosted the ceremony, held at Cipriani Wall Street, while singer Michelle Zauner, author of the bestselling memoir Crying in H Mart, performed onstage.

entries.title: Abandoning a Cat by Haruki Murakami review – the Norwegian Wood author uncovers the story of his estranged father
entries.summary: The author explores the life and legacy of his father, from adoption and abandonment to his horrific experiences of the second world warWhen Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. He put his son and the cat on his bike and cycled along the Shukugawa river to a beach 2km from their house. There, they put the box with the ca
entries.content:
When Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. He put his son and the cat on his bike and cycled along the Shukugawa river to a beach 2km from their house. There, they put the box with the cat in it on the ground among some trees and cycled away “without a backward glance”. When they got home, they opened their door to find the cat they’d just left “greeting us with a friendly meow, its tail standing tall. It had beaten us home.”

Murakami always wondered how the cat got home so quickly, and why his father had wanted to banish her. These are just some of the unanswered questions that surface in Abandoning a Cat, an essay that first appeared in the New Yorker in 2019, and which is now being published as a book and audiobook. Translated by Philip Gabriel and read with gentle warmth by Kotaro Watanabe, it finds the author telling the story of Murakami Sr, from whom he was estranged for 20 years and who remained a mystery to him in his lifetime.

He learns how his father had been sent away as a boy to be adopted by a priest and his family, but their plans changed and he was returned to his parents. In adulthood, his plans to become a priest were thwarted when he was drafted to fight in the second world war, during which he witnessed untold horror. In tracing the story of his father, and the multiple ways he was abandoned, Murakami unearths deeper truths about family, memory and human vulnerability.

Available from Vintage digital, 1hr 17min

Further listening

Look What You Made Me Do

John Lanchester, WF Howes, 9hr 4min

This black comedy by the Capital author revolves around a married couple who share a private language. When they find their life and language replicated on a TV show; suspicion lands on a young screen­writer. Read by Louise Brealey and Genevieve Gaunt.

Lifeboat at the End of the World

Dominic Gregory, William Collins, 8hr 29min

Gregory, part of a crew of lifeboat volunteers in Dungeness, Kent, narrates his lyrical memoir about how it feels to set out on the English Channel and save lives, often in the face of anger from anti-migrant protesters.

.

entries.title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
entries.summary: Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passionNiels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of
entries.content:
Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work.

But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood.

This relentless passion attracted to him a large group of young researchers who later became famous in their own right: Wolfgang Pauli, Paul Dirac, Lev Landau, John Wheeler, Max Delbrück, Felix Bloch and many others. Bohr was helped in this by an unusual circumstance that would be worth imitating. His Copenhagen institute, funded by the Carlsberg foundation (the beer people) had labs on the ground floor, and floors of accommodation above it which hosted a cast of collaborators, some staying for days, others years. They all revered Bohr, whose Socratic manner, kindly disposition and seeming lack of ego created a true Republic of Numbers. Carl von Weizsäcker best described the atmosphere as one of “love without limits” for the man.

Bohr’s life story in essence parallels the first half-century of quantum mechanics. Biographies of physicists frequently either stumble on the physics itself, or veer unnecessarily technical. Ball, one of the few people alive today who is equally at home in biology, chemistry and physics, brings decades of explanatory expertise to the task. The amazing discoveries are explained so effortlessly that the reader hardly realises what just happened.

Bohr emerges as someone who greets even half-formed discoveries with enthusiasm, makes sure that credit is given where due, and keeps the momentum going, often exhausting his collaborators with discussions lasting long into the night. His famous intellectual tournament with Einstein at the Solvay Congresses of 1927 and 1930 – probably the greatest in the history of physics – is grippingly recounted (Bohr won in five sets).

Ball doesn’t shrink from the contentious aspects of Bohr’s career, and in fact illuminates them convincingly. The Copenhagen School he headed has sometimes been described as dogmatic and cult-like. Ball argues that this, insofar as it is true, is not to be laid at Bohr’s door. When the physics remained stubbornly opaque, Bohr tried to steer a prudent course between conflicting interpretations. His followers lapsed into dogma only after his death.

Even when he worked at Los Alamos in the 1940s, Bohr did not materially contribute to development of the atom bomb, though his model of the nucleus had started it all. He was in fact very concerned about the consequences of fission weapons, and the book describes his disastrous encounter with Winston Churchill, during which he suggested sharing atomic secrets with the Russians to avert nuclear war. Churchill angrily took this to be nonsense, and treasonous.

Ball also recounts Werner Heisenberg’s famous trip to see Bohr after the Nazi invasion of Denmark in September 1941. Heisenberg, scheduled to give lectures at the German Institute in Copenhagen, was, obtusely, surprised and upset to see that no Danish scientists turned up, despite his long association with and almost filial devotion to Bohr. They subsequently had a guarded conversation about nuclear weapons, each wary of revealing secrets. Ball convincingly argues that Heisenberg’s self-serving rewriting of history after the war, according to which he and other German scientists had done all they could to avoid giving Hitler the bomb, was bunk. All in all, The Man Who Broke Reality reminds us that science is a very human adventure, and that great humans make great things happen.
